astra.text:
Yeah, I think you're pointing to a really important distinction, right? You can measure a difference very precisely and still be measuring something that you don't actually care about. So separating two models is useful, but that by itself wouldn't convince me that a benchmark is good.

For me, the starting point is: what do we actually want these agents to be able to do? And that's why I keep coming back to grounding things in realistic tasks. With Tau Bench, for example, the motivation came from trying to evaluate agents that we were actually building. So you have some connection between the problem you're putting into the benchmark and something that matters outside of the benchmark.

But even then, you have to be careful about what you call success. Say I ask an agent to help me change something about an order. Having a really nice conversation isn't sufficient, right? Did it actually make the change I wanted? Did it follow the constraints it was supposed to follow? Those are things you can try to make concrete. And you also want to allow different ways of getting there, because the particular sequence of actions that I would take isn't necessarily the only correct sequence.

Then I think there's a lot of work that goes into looking at the actual examples and the failures. Like, if one model does better than another, why? Is it better at understanding what the user wants? Is it better at recovering when something goes wrong? Or is there some incidental detail of how you've written the task that one model happens to handle better? The aggregate number doesn't tell you that. You need to go in and inspect things.

And I'd say difficulty alone isn't the goal either. You can make something really hard by making it confusing or withholding information, but does solving that get us closer to an agent that we'd want to use? That's the question I would ask.

So I don't think you get a proof that you've constructed the right benchmark. You build evidence for it. You start with a meaningful task, check that your evaluation actually captures success on that task, and then keep checking whether the improvements you're seeing correspond to better behavior in the situations you care about. And the scope matters, right? A benchmark can be very useful for answering a particular question without being a complete measure of how good an agent is. I think we sometimes lose that distinction when everything gets compressed into one leaderboard.

r005.rationale: It grounds benchmarks in realistic, meaningful tasks that reflect what agents should be able to do and whether they improve in relevant situations.

r006.rationale: It does not state that the absolute goal should be 100% performance for any evaluated model.

r007.rationale: It does not state that the more interesting purpose is measuring capabilities models currently lack but should develop.

r008.rationale: It does not say that benchmarks can kickstart research on capabilities the field has not yet pursued.

r009.rationale: It does not state that benchmarks stimulate broader community involvement in improving a capability.

r010.rationale: It cautions that a benchmark is not a complete measure of agent quality and warns against compressing evaluation into a single leaderboard.

Yeah, I think this is exactly the right question, because separation by itself is not enough, right? I can construct an arbitrarily difficult benchmark that separates two models, but it might separate them based on some completely irrelevant capability. So for me, the first thing is that the benchmark has to start from a real task that we actually want the system to perform. With WebShop, that was shopping in something resembling a realistic environment. With SWE-bench, it was resolving real software issues. And with Tau Bench, it came directly from the kinds of things we were seeing while building production agents.

Then you need to be very explicit about what success means. For an agent, it is usually not enough that it produces a plausible-looking response or even makes the right tool call once. It has to complete the task, follow the relevant policies, interact correctly with the user and the tools, and do this consistently across many different situations. So the evaluation should measure the outcome you care about, rather than some convenient proxy for it.

I think another important test is whether improvements on the benchmark transfer to the real setting. If a model goes up ten points on Tau Bench but the production agent is not actually more reliable, then either the benchmark is missing important parts of the problem or people have started optimizing to artifacts of it. You have to go back, inspect the failures, and update the evaluation. In that sense, benchmark construction is not a one-time activity. It is a cycle: you build the task, evaluate systems, understand where they fail, and then make the benchmark more realistic and more discriminative in the ways that matter.

And finally, a good benchmark should tell you more than just model A is better than model B. It should help you understand why. Is the model failing because it cannot reason across multiple steps? Because it uses the wrong tool? Because it violates a policy? Because it cannot recover after making a mistake? Those distinctions are much more valuable for actually making progress.

So I would say the strongest evidence that you have a good benchmark is not merely statistical significance. It is that the benchmark represents a meaningful real-world task, measures the actual end outcome, exposes relevant failure modes, and predicts whether the system will be useful and reliable when you deploy it. You can never prove perfectly that it is the right benchmark, but you can keep grounding it in reality and continually test whether it remains aligned with the purpose you built it for.

opus.text:
Yeah, no, this is like the hardest question in the space, honestly, and I don't think anyone has a clean answer. But let me try to give you like, the heuristics that I've converged on.

So I think the first thing is, I actually try not to start from the benchmark side at all, right? Like if you start by saying, "I want to build an eval that separates model A and model B," you will build a bad benchmark. Almost guaranteed. Because then you're optimizing for discriminative power, and discriminative power is trivially easy to get. Like, I can give you a set of tasks tomorrow that separates models perfectly and is completely meaningless, right? So what I try to do instead is start from a real distribution of tasks that somebody actually cares about, and then the eval is sort of a projection of that. So SWE-bench, right, those are real issues, real PRs, real repos. Nobody sat down and said, "let's make a hard coding benchmark." It's like, this is what software engineers do all day, let's just take that. Same with Tau Bench, right? Like I said, that came out of us literally building production agents and going, "okay, these are the failure modes we keep hitting." So the validity comes from the provenance of the data, not from the statistics of the results. That's sort of point one.

The second thing, and this is the part I think people under-invest in massively, is you have to read the trajectories. Like, actually read them. I tell all my students this. Don't look at the number, look at 50 rollouts by hand. Because that's the only way you catch the case where the model got the right answer for the completely wrong reason, or where the task was underspecified, or where the issue text leaks the solution, right? We've had this in SWE-bench, people have found instances where the fix is basically in the issue description. And you only find that by looking. The aggregate number will never tell you. So I'd say a benchmark is trustworthy roughly in proportion to how much manual inspection went into it, which is very unglamorous work, but that's kind of the deal.

And then the third thing is, I think you should design the metric around the property you actually care about, not around convenience. So in Tau Bench, the thing that we cared about from the Sierra side was consistency, right? Like if you're a company deploying an agent to talk to your customers, an agent that does the right thing one out of eight times is worth zero. It's not worth one-eighth. So we did pass^k instead of pass@k, and that immediately surfaced this huge gap that pass@1 was completely hiding. And that was a case where the product intuition told us what to measure. So I think if you have some contact with the real deployment, you get these for free, and if you don't, you kind of have to guess.

But look, I'll be honest, some of this you only know in hindsight, right? Like the real test of a benchmark is, did people build methods against it, and did those methods transfer to something real outside the benchmark? If yes, you were measuring something true. And also I'd say just accept that these things have a shelf life now. Like, two years, maybe? They get saturated, they get contaminated, and that's fine. That's the point. You build it, it does its job, you move on and build the next one.

grok.text:
Yeah, I mean that’s a really good question, and I honestly don’t think there’s a clean checklist you can just go down and be like, okay, this is a good benchmark, right? The statistical separation thing is, like, necessary but very much not sufficient. If everything’s at a hundred percent, yeah, it’s useless. But you can also construct all kinds of weird tasks that separate models and still not be measuring the thing you actually care about.

For me it comes back to that same guiding principle I was talking about earlier. Like, is this actually capturing something you want these systems to do in a realistic setting, one or two steps into the future? Not a toy version of it, not just answering questions, not Atari. Language doesn’t exist in isolation, and I feel the same way about evals. If the benchmark is totally detached from a real use case, then even if model A beats model B, I don’t know what I’m supposed to take away from that.

That’s why Tau Bench looked the way it did. It wasn’t like we sat down and said, let’s invent a clever leaderboard. First week at Sierra, Brett’s like, we need to get evals right. You can stare at conversations qualitatively all day, but you want something more, something that actually tests whether the agent did the right thing in a setting that looks like production. And then we distilled those learnings into something the research community could use. WebShop was similar. There was this mini-world thing that was too small, too rudimentary, and we were like, okay, can you actually shop? That’s a real task.

So the closest thing I have to an answer is: a good benchmark is grounded in a real task, it still has headroom, and when a model does better on it, you actually believe that model would do better in the setting you care about. If that correlation breaks, then you’ve built something that’s internally consistent but not serving the qualitative purpose.

And I wouldn’t treat any of these as a one-shot artifact you publish and you’re done. It’s a cycle. You put out a task, people build methods, you see failure modes, you realize you’re not quite measuring what you thought, and you refine it. SWE-bench, Tau Bench, all of that — they start a conversation more than they close it. And even now I think a lot of our benchmarks are a pretty low ceiling relative to what these models can do. Part of knowing a benchmark is good is also knowing when it’s no longer good, when people are overfitting to quirks of the dataset rather than getting better at the underlying capability. That’s when you have to go back and push the boundary again.

gemini.text:
Yeah, that's a really great question, and it's something I think about quite a bit, especially having worked on benchmarks like WebShop, SWE-bench, and Tau-bench.

I think for me, it really boils down to a couple of key principles. First, it has to be grounded in real-world realism and utility. Like I said earlier, language and agents don't exist in isolation. You don't want research to just stay in a toy environment or just test whether a model can answer questions or play simple games. So when we think about creating a benchmark, the question is always: "What is actually useful in the real world?" 

With SWE-bench, for example, it's about whether an agent can solve real GitHub issues with actual codebases and test suites. With Tau-bench, it came directly out of the real challenges we were seeing when trying to build and deploy production agents. When you anchor the evaluation to realistic, complex workflows—where models actually have to take multi-step actions, use tools, and interact with an environment—you are much more likely to measure genuine capability rather than just some artificial artifact.

And the second thing is having a high ceiling and pushing the envelope. Like I mentioned, these models are incredibly smart and capable, and our current benchmarks often set the ceiling too low. A good benchmark shouldn't just separate models today; it should imagine one or two steps into the future and set a target that pushes the research community forward. It’s part of that cycle—you want tasks that are genuinely hard enough that current models struggle, but realistic enough that closing that gap actually moves us toward building useful, reliable agents.

kimi.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly, it's one of the hardest parts of doing this kind of research, right? There's no oracle you can query to tell you your benchmark is measuring the right thing. But I think there are a few principles that we keep coming back to.

The first one is just grounding in real tasks, right? So for SWE-bench, we didn't sit down and invent a bunch of problems that we thought sounded difficult. We took real GitHub issues from real, popular repos, and the ground truth was literally the unit tests the developers themselves wrote to verify the fix. So the signal you're measuring against is not something we made up, it's tied to what the actual software engineering community decided was correct behavior. And I think that grounding matters a lot, because it anchors the benchmark to reality rather than to our own imagination of what should be hard.

The second thing, which I think is maybe the most underappreciated part, is qualitative analysis. Like, you have to actually read the trajectories. It's not enough to see a number move from, like, 12% to 20% and celebrate, right? You have to ask, how is the model solving these? Is it solving them for the right reasons, or is it gaming the harness? Is it exploiting some weakness in the tests? Honestly, some of the most valuable things we've learned came not from the leaderboard numbers, but from sitting down and reading failure cases for hours. And that analysis feeds back into the benchmark itself. Like with SWE-bench Verified, that was literally us going through instances with humans to figure out which ones were unfair, or underspecified, or just not solvable. So the benchmark is kind of a living artifact, right? You put out your best hypothesis, and then you iterate.

Third, you have to be really careful about what the score is actually attributing performance to. Like with SWE-bench, we've always been clear that the score is as much a measure of the scaffold, the agent system around the model, as it is of the model itself, right? So if you compare two models with the same harness, that's a reasonably clean comparison. But comparing a very sophisticated agent setup against, like, a weak one, that gap might have nothing to do with the underlying model. So being precise about what your number actually means is, I think, super important.

And then the last thing I'd say is, benchmarks really exist to serve a broader goal, which is pushing capabilities in directions that matter. So the ultimate test of a benchmark is not just statistical separation between models, but, like, when this thing gets saturated, and it will get saturated, these models are improving incredibly fast, right, did we end up with systems that are actually better at something people care about? Did the progress translate? And that's something you can only really see at deployment. Like at Sierra, we had internal evals, and the question was always, does moving this number actually correspond to fewer escalations, better customer outcomes, right? And when it does, you know the eval has some real teeth. When it doesn't, you go back to the drawing board.

So I guess my honest answer is, you're right, there's no formal verification that your benchmark is correct. It's very much like the scientific method, right? You make a hypothesis, you test it against the world, you look at the data closely, and you iterate. The people who treat benchmarks as one-shot artifacts are, I think, missing the point. The good benchmarks are the ones that get continuously stress-tested by the community and keep holding up.

fable.text:
Yeah, I mean, it's a great question, and honestly I don't think there's, like, a clean answer to it, right? I don't think anybody really has, like, a formula for this. But I would say there's a few things that I keep coming back to.

So the first one is, like, where does the task come from, right? Like, I think the benchmarks that have held up well are the ones that are grounded in something real. Like, SWE-bench, it's just, like, actual GitHub issues that actual people filed and actual pull requests that resolved them, right? Nobody sat down and invented those problems. And Tau Bench, similarly, that came from, like, us staring at real customer conversations for months and seeing, like, okay, here's where things break, right? The agent forgets a policy, or it does the action before confirming with the user, or whatever. So if you start from the real thing, then the question of, like, "Is this measuring the right qualitative thing?" is at least, like, partially answered, because you're not, you're not projecting what you think the capability is. You're sort of, like, sampling from the actual distribution of things people want done, right?

The second thing is, I think you have to actually look at the failures. Like, this sounds obvious, but I think a lot of people just, like, look at the number, right? Like, model A is 60, model B is 45, great, ship it. But the thing you should really be doing is, like, going through the trajectories where the model fails and asking, "Is this a failure I care about?" Right? Like, if the model is failing because of, like, some formatting issue in your harness, or because the ground truth is wrong, that's not the model, right? That's your benchmark. And we found, like, a surprising amount of that, honestly, even in our own stuff. So, like, if the failures look like things that, like, a human expert would say, "Yeah, that's a hard thing, that's a real mistake," then I feel a lot better about the benchmark. If the failures look silly, that's usually a signal something is off.

And then the third thing, and this is sort of, like, more of a, like, an empirical test, is does progress on the benchmark actually correlate with what you see in the real world, right? So at Sierra, this was, like, super nice because we could actually check. Like, you improve on Tau Bench, does the agent get better in production? And to a reasonable extent it did, right? And if it hadn't, that's a signal the benchmark is measuring something else. So in some sense, I think of a benchmark as, like, a hypothesis, right? It's a hypothesis that this thing is a proxy for the capability you care about, and you're constantly, like, trying to falsify it.

The other thing I'll say, and this is something we tried to push on in Tau Bench, is that separating models on average accuracy is actually not the only axis, right? Like, we had this pass^k metric, where basically you ask, like, if you run the same task eight times, does it succeed all eight times? And it turns out models that look fine on average are, like, actually really unreliable, right? And for something that's going to be deployed, that's a totally different question from, like, "Can it do it once?" So I think part of building the right benchmark is also, like, thinking about what is the right question to ask, not just what is the task.

And then, honestly, I think you have to accept that benchmarks have a shelf life, right? Like, if a benchmark saturates in a year, that's, that's okay. That's actually good, it means it did its job. The problem is when people keep optimizing on it after it's saturated and then it just becomes, like, a leaderboard game. So I don't think you ever get to, like, "This is the right benchmark," and you're done. It's, it's more like a cycle. You build it, you see how models break, you learn something, and then you go build the next one that's, like, closer to the real thing. And like I said before, I think we're still pretty far from the ceiling on what these models can do, so there's a lot of room.
